hook: A new ramen shop opens and has a line out the door for months. Then three more ramen shops open within a few blocks, each a little different. A year later the first shop is still busy, but its owner is earning only what she could earn elsewhere. Many sellers, slightly different products and easy entry: that is monopolistic competition.

ideas: Monopolistic competition: many firms, differentiated products, easy entry and exit. Each firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve with MR below it.
Short run: produce where MR = MC, price from demand; profit or loss is $(P - \text{ATC}) \times Q$, as for a monopolist.
Long run: entry (or exit) shifts each firm's demand until it is tangent to ATC: P = ATC, zero economic profit.
At the tangency P > MC (not allocatively efficient) and output is below minimum ATC: excess capacity (not productively efficient). The trade: more variety.

misconception.wrong: In the long run a monopolistically competitive firm ends up at the minimum of ATC, like a perfectly competitive firm.
misconception.right: Zero economic profit means P = ATC, and a downward-sloping demand curve can touch the U-shaped ATC only where ATC is still falling. So the firm produces less than the output at minimum ATC: excess capacity.

summary: In monopolistic competition, many firms sell differentiated products and entry is easy. Each firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve, produces where MR = MC and reads its price from demand, so in the short run it can earn a profit or make a loss. Profit draws entry and losses cause exit, shifting each firm's demand until it is tangent to ATC: zero economic profit. At that point price is above marginal cost and output is below the minimum of ATC (excess capacity), the cost of the variety buyers enjoy.
